subject: physics
title: Required practicals: mechanics and materials
key_idea: These practicals measure g from a falling object, the Young modulus of a wire, and, for some courses, viscosity, force and change of momentum, and collisions. Each one needs a clear method, a graph with a useful gradient, and a sensible estimate of the uncertainty.

sections.heading: Measuring the acceleration of free fall

blocks.text: Drop an object from a measured height and time the fall. A free-falling object accelerates at g.

blocks.label: Distance fallen from rest
where: g = acceleration of free fall, in m/s²
t = time of fall, in s

items.text: Hold a small dense ball with an electromagnet at the top. Place a trapdoor switch, linked to a timer, on the floor below.
Measure the height s from the bottom of the ball to the trapdoor with a metre rule or tape.
Switch off the electromagnet. The timer starts at the same moment and stops when the ball hits the trapdoor.
Repeat each height several times and take the mean time. Then change the height.
Plot s against t². The graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient g/2.
g = 2 × gradient.

diagram.alt: A slider for a ball dropped from a chosen height. It shows the time recorded and the value of g calculated from it, and how a small delay in the timing lowers the calculated g.

inputs.label: Delay in timing (timer reads too long)

items: Use a small, dense ball so that air resistance is small.
Using several heights and a graph is better than one height, because it averages random errors and shows up anomalous results.
The time is squared, so a percentage uncertainty in t is **doubled** in g.
A delay in the switch or timer is a systematic error. It makes the calculated g too low. Plotting √s against t gives a straight line with gradient √(g/2), and the delay shows as an intercept.
Time the fall from rest over different heights.
Plot s against t². The gradient is g/2.

sections.heading: Measuring the Young modulus of a wire

blocks.text: Stretch a long, thin wire with known loads. Measure the extension and the wire's diameter.

items.text: Fix a long thin wire to a firm support. Hang a weight hanger on the other end and mark a point on the wire next to a ruler.
Measure the original length L with a metre rule. Measure the diameter d at several places with a micrometer.
Add equal masses. After each, record the new position of the marker. Extension = new length − original length.
Plot force F against extension ΔL. The straight part has gradient F/ΔL.
E = gradient × L / A, where A = πd² / 4.

items: Measure the diameter in several places and in two directions, and take the mean. The area depends on d², so d is the biggest source of uncertainty.
Use loads that stay within the limit of proportionality, so that the wire is not permanently stretched.
Hang a small initial load first, so that the wire is straight before the first reading.
A long wire gives a larger extension that is easier to measure.
Measure L, the diameter and the extension for a range of loads.
E = gradient of the force–extension graph × L / A.

checks.q: In an experiment to find g, a ball is dropped from several heights s and the time t is measured. State the graph you would plot and how g is found.
checks.a: Plot s against t². The graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient g/2, so g = 2 × gradient.

checks.q: Explain why the diameter of a wire must be measured carefully in an experiment to find the Young modulus.
checks.a: The area A is proportional to d², so a given percentage uncertainty in d gives double that percentage uncertainty in A and in E. The diameter is therefore usually the largest source of uncertainty.

checks.q: Give two ways to improve the accuracy of an experiment to find the Young modulus of a wire.
checks.a: Any two from: use a longer wire so the extension is larger; measure the diameter at several places and take a mean; use a micrometer for the diameter; use a range of loads and a graph; stay within the limit of proportionality.

blocks.text: Viscosity of a liquid with a falling ball

items.text: Fill a tall transparent tube with the liquid. Mark two lines well below the surface, far enough down that the ball has reached terminal velocity.
Measure the distance between the marks. Measure the ball's diameter with a micrometer.
Drop the ball and time it between the marks with a stopwatch. Repeat and take a mean.
Terminal velocity v = distance ÷ time.

blocks.label: Viscosity from terminal velocity
where: η = viscosity of the liquid, in Pa s
r = radius of the ball, in m
ρₛ = density of the ball, in kg/m³
ρₗ = density of the liquid, in kg/m³

items: At terminal velocity the weight equals the upthrust plus the viscous drag.
Use balls of different radius and plot v against r². The graph is a straight line through the origin.
Viscosity falls as the temperature rises, so keep the temperature constant and record it.

items.text: Pull a trolley along a track with a string over a pulley and a hanging mass. Put light gates on the track.
Record the speeds at the gates and the time between them. Δp = m(v − u), where m is the total mass of trolley and hanger.
Change the force by moving masses from the trolley to the hanger so the total mass stays the same.
Plot the force against Δp/Δt. The graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient 1, showing F = Δp/Δt.

blocks.text: Collisions between small spheres using ICT

items.text: Film a collision of two ball bearings on a table top from above, with a ruler in view and a known frame rate.
Use software to find the position of each ball in every frame. The software gives the velocity from the change in position over the frame time.
Calculate the total momentum and total kinetic energy before and after the collision.

items: If total momentum is the same, momentum has been conserved. Resolve into components for a two-dimensional collision.
If total kinetic energy is the same, the collision is elastic.
The camera must be directly above, and the table level, so that the velocities are measured correctly.
